transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I... I suppose I'm here because things have been getting complicated at work. I work as a cashier, you see, and normally it's fine, it's just scanning and bagging, but lately... lately I keep getting stuck. It’s hard to explain, but I’ll be right in the middle of a transaction, and suddenly I’m just doing things that don’t fit the moment at all. Like, the other day, I had this whole line of people, and instead of scanning the milk, I just started tapping the scanner with the barcode, over and over, in this very specific pattern. It felt like I had to finish the pattern before I could move on, but the customer was just staring at me. And then sometimes I just freeze entirely. I’ll have my hand hovering right over the open cash drawer, holding a ten-dollar bill, and I just stop. I can’t move my arm, I can’t hand them the change, I’m just suspended there while they’re waiting and staring. It’s incredibly embarrassing, and my manager noticed, of course. Last week, she actually wrote me up for it. She said I was being disruptive and unprofessional, but I’m not trying to be. It’s just like my body decides to do these things, or stop doing things, and I’m just stuck there while the world keeps moving around me. It’s really starting to become a problem.
Outside of work, do you ever find yourself making repetitive movements or doing things in a very specific way, even if you don’t want to?

Outside of work? No... no, I haven't noticed anything like that at all. It's actually something I’ve spent a good deal of time thinking about, because you would think if your body is going to start acting up or doing these strange things, it would do it everywhere, right? But when I’m at home—I have a small one-bedroom apartment just a few miles from the store, I've been renting there for about six years now—everything is completely normal. 

I can just sit in my armchair and read. I have a Bachelor's degree, you know, in history, so I do a lot of reading, mostly biographies and historical non-fiction, and I can just turn the pages without any trouble. I don't get stuck holding the page halfway through turning it. I don't start tapping the spine of the book. I just read. And when I go into the kitchen to make dinner—usually just something simple, I'm not much of a cook, maybe heating up some soup or making a turkey sandwich—I just do it. I open the fridge, I get the mayonnaise, I close the fridge. I never just stand there with my hand hovering over the jar like I do with the cash drawer. 

It’s like my apartment is this safe zone where my brain and my hands actually communicate the way they’re supposed to. I can do my laundry, I can water my spider plant, I can brush my teeth, all without any of that freezing or the repetitive tapping. It’s really only when I’m on the clock, standing on that anti-fatigue mat behind register four, that things go haywire. So, no, to answer your question, when I'm on my own time, I just go about my day completely normally. Which, honestly, just makes the whole situation at the store that much more frustrating and baffling to me, because I know I'm capable of functioning just fine.

When these episodes happen at work—when you're tapping the scanner in a pattern or freezing with the cash in your hand—do you feel spaced out, detached, or like you're watching yourself from the outside?

No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Actually, it's quite the opposite. I am completely, painfully aware of exactly where I am and what is happening. I'm not floating above register four looking down at myself, and I'm not in some sort of fog or dream state. I am right there in my own shoes. 

I can feel the rubber of the anti-fatigue mat under my feet—I wear these special orthotic inserts because standing for eight hours a day at my age really does a number on your arches, you know, but I can feel them pressing into my heels the whole time. And I can hear absolutely everything. I hear the hum of the fluorescent lights overhead, I hear the constant *beep, beep, beep* coming from the other lanes, the squeak of the conveyor belts, the music on the overhead speakers... all of it. 

When I was frozen with that ten-dollar bill last week, I was looking right at the customer. She was wearing a blue raincoat, even though it wasn't raining that day, which I remember thinking was a bit odd, and she had this expression on her face. At first, it was just mild impatience, like she was in a hurry, maybe running late to pick up her kids or get to an appointment, but then it shifted to this deep, uncomfortable confusion as I just stood there. And I saw all of that happen in real-time. I felt the crisp paper of the money in my fingers. I was practically screaming at my arm inside my head, just begging it to extend forward, telling myself to just hand her the change so we could both move on with our lives. But it just wouldn't obey. 

So, no, I don't feel spaced out or detached in the slightest. Honestly, if I did, maybe it wouldn't be quite so awful! If I was spaced out, maybe I wouldn't feel the sheer, agonizing embarrassment of the situation. But I'm fully present, locked inside myself, just... waiting for my body to let me finish the transaction. It's like being a prisoner in your own muscles, but your mind is completely sharp and awake the entire time, taking in every single humiliating detail.
